Dharohar Commerce Exchange: The Intake Decision

What the evidence says about product-management hiring, and what it does not

1. Opening

On Monday 5 October 2026, Devyani Phadke, head of talent at Dharohar Commerce Exchange, sat in a glass meeting room at the company's Pune headquarters with a one-page hiring plan and a deadline. The board's people committee would meet on Thursday 15 October, and it expected a single recommendation on how many product managers to hire in the financial year ahead, at what levels, and from where.

The plan on the page called for fourteen product-management openings. Six were for associate product managers, five for mid-level product managers with three to seven years of experience, and three for senior product managers. Two weeks earlier, the chief product officer had written in the planning thread: "Every credible founder I speak to says the junior PM role is finished. Why are we signing six offers for it?"

2. Company background

Dharohar Commerce Exchange, founded in Pune in 2013, runs a business-to-business procurement exchange for small retailers. About 38,000 neighbourhood stores, from kirana shops to pharmacies and stationers, use its app to order from regional distributors, compare prices and draw short-term credit. It connects to the Open Network for Digital Commerce, takes payments over UPI, and reported revenue of ₹640 crore in the last financial year. It employs about 1,900 people, of whom 46 work in product management.

The competition is crowded and well funded. Udaan and Flipkart's wholesale arm chase the same retailers; Reliance Retail's JioMart Partners programme approaches them through distributors; and Zepto and Swiggy Instamart pull shoppers away from the kirana counter altogether. Dharohar competes for PM talent with those firms and with Razorpay, PhonePe, Zomato, Freshworks, Zoho and Postman, and recruits each year from ISB, the IIMs and the engineering colleges that supply Infosys and TCS.

3. The situation

Devyani had spent the previous month collecting what was measured and separating it from what was merely repeated. The public claims were loud and contradictory. Founders on stage said that coding agents let one product manager and two engineers do what ten people once did. Recruiters on professional networks said PM postings had thinned.

The firm's own records were the one dataset she could trust, and Exhibit 1 sets them out. Openings fell from 20 in FY25 to 16 in FY26, which fits the shrinking story. Applications rose over the same three years, from 5,400 to 11,200, so applications per opening more than doubled, from 300 to 700. Figure 1 draws that last column. A reader hunting for collapse sees fewer posts. A reader hunting for stability sees a talent pool that keeps arriving. Both are reading the same table.

Gitanjali Moreira, the talent analyst in Melbourne, added a complication. Her screening tool flagged 4,256 of the 11,200 FY26 applications, 38 per cent, for template-like case-study answers. Rising volume therefore measured the falling cost of applying at least as much as it measured any rise in the supply of capable candidates. The same technology that worried the chief product officer was inflating the applicant count and weakening the screen at the same time.

Exhibit 2 shows who actually joined in FY26 and what they cost. Twelve people came on board: five associates, four mid-level and three senior product managers, at a total annual cost to company of ₹452 lakh, an average of ₹37.7 lakh each.

The distant members of the team saw the market differently. Daniela Rocha, who runs seller onboarding from Lisbon, reported that European start-ups were advertising fewer entry-level product roles, but she also pointed out that European funding had tightened, and that rising interest rates since 2022 had cut hiring in every function.

That left a short ledger. What was measured: openings at Dharohar fell, applications rose, and screening quality dropped. What was asserted: that AI was the cause, that the effect lands on juniors, and that it will persist. What was unknown: whether FY26's drop in openings was a trend or a dip, because only three data points existed.

4. The people

Gaurang Sabnis, chief product officer, based in Bengaluru, wanted a lean team and was prepared to bet early. He argued that six associate offers were six salaries for work a senior product manager with good tooling could now do alone, and that a freeze would send a useful signal to the market and to the board.

Dhruv Kesarkar, vice president of engineering in Pune, wanted fewer product managers at any level. His engineers were building prototypes in days, and he felt that decisions, not specifications, were now the bottleneck.

Gitanjali Moreira, talent analyst in Melbourne, wanted a decision the data could later judge. She pressed for explicit review dates and for a selection process that tested candidates on live work rather than on take-home essays that an assistant could now write.

Daniela Rocha, onboarding lead in Lisbon, wanted a pipeline. She had seen her own early-career hires grow into the people who now ran Dharohar's seller programmes, and she doubted that a company could buy that judgement from outside at the same price.

5. The options

Devyani framed three courses of action, costed in Exhibit 3. The FY27 baseline of 14 openings at FY26 pay bands costs ₹508 lakh.

Option A: freeze the associate intake. Hire no associates, convert the six associate slots into two additional senior roles, and hire five mid-level and five senior product managers. This is ten hires at ₹540 lakh. It bets everything on a trend that the firm has measured for only one year, costs more than the baseline, and leaves nobody coming up behind the seniors.

Option B: hold the plan. Hire all fourteen as planned, at ₹508 lakh, on the view that the evidence for change is thin. This preserves the pipeline but ignores a live screening problem.

Option C: stage the intake and fix the selection. Hire three associates now, along with the five mid-level and three senior roles, and hold the other three associate slots until a review in January. Spend ₹6 lakh to replace take-home essays with a supervised live product exercise. This is eleven hires at ₹454 lakh in pay plus ₹6 lakh for the assessment, ₹460 lakh in all. Its upside is that it preserves the pipeline, improves the screen, and generates evidence. Its cost is complexity, and a delay that some strong candidates will not wait for.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using only the three years in Exhibit 1, which statements about PM hiring can Dharohar support, and which are assertions? What would the same table need to contain before it could prove a trend?

2. Applications per opening rose from 300 to 700 while 38 per cent of the FY26 applications looked templated. What does the number actually measure, and how should Devyani use it?

3. Gaurang's claim is about the entry level. Which evidence would separate the effect of cheap AI building from the effect of tight funding, and who at Dharohar could collect it?

4. Which option should Devyani take to the committee on 15 October, and which observable results in January would make her change course?

7. A note for the learner

This topic asks the learner to hold a calibrated view. The two loud stories, collapse and no change, are both stronger than the data permits. What the firm can say is narrower: its openings fell, its application volume rose, its screen weakened, and it has three years of history. A well-reasoned answer names those facts, labels the causal claims as hypotheses, and chooses an action that stays sound under either story.

One defensible path is Option C. It is cheaper than the baseline by ₹48 lakh and cheaper than Option A by ₹80 lakh, and it does not stake the pipeline on an unproven trend. More important, it converts uncertainty into evidence: Devyani can write down in October what she expects to see by January, such as the offer-acceptance rate, how the new live exercise ranks candidates against the old essays, and whether associates hired in the first window are producing work that a senior would otherwise have done. If those results show no value in associates, the three held slots are released into mid-level roles; if they show value, the slots are filled, and the intake has been protected.

Option A and Option B each lock in a conclusion that three data points cannot yet carry, and no one yet knows how much of any decline in postings is the technology and how much is the cost of money.

PM Hiring: What the Evidence Says and What It Doesn’t

AI & Data Products › How AI Is Changing PM Practice

1. Two product leaders, two weeks apart

On Thursday, 10 September 2026, Oindrila Sanyal had nine approved requisitions and no confidence in any of them. She ran product at Rupak Banking Systems, a Chennai firm selling core-ledger software to Indian banks, with a delivery pod in Rotterdam under Roosmarijn Bakker. Her chief executive had asked a question she could not answer from the inside: are we hiring into a profession that is still growing, or are we the last firm on the platform?

Four of the nine seats were associate product manager roles. Rupak’s associate population had fallen from twelve people to five over thirty months, not by decision but by attrition nobody backfilled. Her recruiting lead, Roshni Panjwani, had funnel data that resisted interpretation: applications per requisition up four-and-a-half-fold, starts down about a fifth.

Two weeks later, on Thursday, 24 September 2026, Pradyumna Ghatge faced the inverse problem in Ahmedabad. As vice-president of product at Patang Instrument Works, which builds cold-chain monitoring hardware and the software that reads it, he had eleven product managers against two hundred and five engineers and three seats empty. One owned the firmware release train gating a March 2027 launch, built with a manufacturer in Osaka under Ryoko Hasegawa.

Omkar Sathaye, his finance director, had drawn the opposite conclusion: if product management is contracting, wait and hire cheaply. Pradyumna believed the empty seat cost more per week than the person cost per quarter. Oindrila’s board met on 8 October 2026.

2. The idea: four quantities, one word

“PM hiring” collapses four quantities that move independently and are measured by instruments of very different quality: a stock (people employed as product managers at a moment), a flow of openings (vacancies being filled over a period, a rate meaningless without its window), a flow of hires (people who start), and a price (what the work pays, by level). The identity binding the first three is rarely written down:

Stock at end = stock at start + hires during the window − separations during the window.

Openings appear nowhere in it; they are an intention, not a transaction. That is why a stock can rise while openings fall, and why both camps quote true numbers at each other indefinitely.

The discipline is borrowed. The Beveridge curve, plotting vacancies against unemployment, dates to British labour economics of the 1940s because vacancies and employment are different objects; the United States built its Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey in 2000 to report openings, hires and separations separately. The task framework of Autor, Levy and Murnane (2003), extended by Acemoglu and Restrepo into displacement and reinstatement effects, supplies the mechanism: a technology removes tasks and adds others, so the net effect is empirical.

India has no equivalent series. The Periodic Labour Force Survey measures employment far above the resolution of “product manager”; the rest is scraped postings, profile data, surveys and anecdote. Four schools contest the question, and the useful exercise is to write down the proposition each would sign and refuse.

The displacement school holds that producing specifications, prototypes and first-draft synthesis has become cheap enough that the junior PM’s task bundle no longer justifies a seat. It signs: entry-level PM openings per rupee of software revenue have fallen and will not recover. It refuses: total PM employment has already fallen.

The composition school holds that demand for product judgement is flat or rising while the mix shifts upward. It signs: PM intensity, product managers per hundred engineers, is flat or rising. It refuses: nothing has changed for someone seeking a first PM job.

The cycle school holds that this is the 2022–24 funding reset in an AI costume. It signs: PM openings track software venture funding with a two-to-three-quarter lag. It refuses: AI has not changed the job’s content.

The identification school, the most uncomfortable and arguably most defensible, holds that no Indian series can distinguish the first three. It signs: no public dataset separates openings from hires for Indian PMs. It refuses: therefore act as though nothing has changed.

3. Mechanics: what an expert actually computes

Roshni’s first move was to compute Rupak’s own identity in six-month windows, because a firm that cannot state its own stock and flows has no standing to interpret anyone else’s.

4. When the evidence applies, and when it misleads

Test one: is the measured quantity the one your decision depends on? Oindrila’s decision turns on whether a PM seat is worth funding in 2029, a question about stock and intensity; posting counts measure openings, so the test fails for her. Pradyumna’s turns on how long one seat stays empty and what that costs, which postings data measures tolerably. The test passes for him.

Test two: is your firm in the sample, and do you need a level or a direction? Rupak recruits by referral and campus, and half its PM hires never reach a public board; Patang recruits in a thin market where almost every role is advertised. Posting indices are in any case useless for level, because de-duplication rules change between vintages.

The evidence turns actively misleading in two cases. First, when a firm’s flows are dominated by noise: Patang’s eleven seats generate perhaps four events a year, so a 25 per cent fall in its hiring is one person changing her mind. Second, when a posting series is used to forecast structural change over a longer horizon than the series itself.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Olakh Identity Services, a Bengaluru firm selling regulated identity verification to lenders and insurers, is the regulated case. Its head of product, Rukhsana Pathan, carries four PMs whose work is largely set by Reserve Bank of India and IRDAI circulars. Those seats cannot be cut on productivity grounds, because their output is the defensibility of a control rather than a volume of features, nor refilled by a generalist in a quarter.

Two-sided businesses create a counting seam rather than a demand effect. Panghat Hiring Exchange, whose posting index half of Indian product leadership quotes, runs twenty-nine PMs across employer tools and candidate experience; one headline count says nothing about which side is growing.

Patang is the hardware case. A launch date set by tooling, certification and channel commitments gives the PM seat on the critical path a shadow price set by slip cost rather than salary band: ₹18 lakh per week.

Pratibimb Vision Labs, a hundred-person computer-vision company founded by Pallavi Ranadive, is the AI-native case and the most misread. It runs six PMs against ninety-four engineers; its intensity is low because the founder still holds most product decisions, a stage effect dressed as a technology effect.

The seam that matters most in India is the internal labour market. In the global capability centres of multinational banks and retailers, most PM seats are filled by internal transfer, appearing neither as external postings nor as profile-level employer changes. Every external index therefore undercounts PM hiring by an amount that grows precisely when firms freeze external hiring.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

A stock can grow while the flow collapses

Rupak’s hiring fell to three in a half-year and its PM population still ended higher than it started, because separations fell too. The tell-tale sign of confusion is a percentage fall in “PM jobs” with no window named: a stock has a date, a flow has a window, and a claim with neither is not a measurement. The obvious reading assumes separations are constant.

Application volume measures the cost of applying

An expert hears “a thousand applications per opening” as a statement about generation cost, not demand. The tell-tale sign is that the ratio of applications to deep-funnel conversions moves while the conversions do not: at Rupak applications rose 275.0 per cent while screen-to-loop conversion fell 2.1 points, from 18.8 to 16.7 per cent.

The right denominator is engineering capacity

Comparing PM postings with all technology postings tells you only whether product fell more or less than its neighbours; what bears on survival is intensity. The comforting reading, that product is holding up because it fell less than engineering, is wrong in direction: if engineering shrinks while roadmaps do not, intensity rises mechanically.

Requisition accounting corrupts counts both ways

One requisition can be posted four times and reposted monthly; one posting can carry three seats; evergreen requisitions harvest pipeline with no funded seat behind them. The tell-tale sign is a series that jumps at quarter boundaries.

Vacancy duration is a demand signal counts suppress

If demand were collapsing, seats would fill fast and cheap. Patang’s median time to fill a senior PM seat was 97 days against 34 for a campus associate, and Rupak’s offer-acceptance rate fell from 82.4 to 68.8 per cent. Falling counts alongside lengthening vacancies signals excess demand for a specific capability.

Cycle and structure share a short-run fingerprint

Over eight quarters a funding contraction and a technological substitution look identical: fewer openings, concentrated at the junior end, pay holding at the top. The only discriminators are cross-sectional and durational, such as comparing product management with a role AI should not touch but capital markets should.

A cohort delay is not a level shift

A firm that skips two associate intakes has not reduced its steady-state PM population; it has created a hole that arrives at the mid-level four years later. Rupak’s associate count fell from 12 to 5, down 58.3 per cent, with no decision ever recorded, and the hole is paid for in 2029 at senior-hire prices.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

The pass rate fell from 15.0 to 6.0 per cent, volume handled rose, deeper rates held, which she read as success. The failure was at the end: of 16 offers only 11 started, against 14 of 17 two years earlier. The screen had optimised for resemblance to past hires.

Rukhsana’s recovery had three parts. She replaced the external index in headcount papers with Olakh’s own stock-flow table; she rebuilt the regulated seats first, accepting the premium; and she ruled that no headcount decision may rest on a series whose de-duplication method is unpublished.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Deciding headcount from a posting index. Early sign: a board paper citing a percentage with no window, level or de-duplication note. Diagnostic: what are your seats-per-requisition and dedupe factors, and did they change? Caught late, the cost is Olakh’s ₹70.0 lakh a year of run-rate.

Reading the application flood as weak demand. Early sign: recruiter pass rates falling while deep-funnel rates hold. Diagnostic: has screen-to-loop conversion moved at all? Caught late, the firm raises its bar until acceptance collapses, as Rupak’s did.

Letting attrition design the ladder. Early sign: an entry level shrinking with no decision in any minute, twelve to five at Rupak. Diagnostic: what is our associate intake plan for the next four intakes, and who owns it? The cost arrives four years later.

Benchmarking against a series you are inside. Early sign: your own postings are a material share of the index you cite. Diagnostic: would this number move if we changed our reposting policy? Panghat cannot use its own index.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The displacement school’s strongest form is not about counts. It is that the junior PM’s apprenticeship, writing the specification and assembling the analysis, was how judgement was acquired, and that mechanism has been priced out; even if seats persist, the ladder does not. It is wrong if firms rebuild apprenticeship around reviewing and editing.

The composition school’s strongest form is the intensity arithmetic: if output per engineer rises and consequential decisions per unit of output do not fall, PMs per engineer must rise, and total demand falls only if engineering shrinks faster. It is wrong if a material share of product decisions is itself automatable.

The cycle school’s strongest form is chronology: the contraction in junior technical hiring began before the tools were capable of the work attributed to them. It is wrong if the junior share fails to recover through a full funding recovery.

The identification school’s strongest form is that none of the three can be tested with Indian data: no openings series with published methodology, no hires series independent of self-reported profiles, no intensity series at all. It is wrong the day a credible panel of firms publishes stock, flows and intensity on a common definition. Until then its counsel, decide under acknowledged uncertainty with tripwires, is the only actionable one, which is not the same as being right.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks “stock, openings, hires or price?” before engaging with any claim, and refuses to proceed until it is answered. They compute their own firm’s identity table before reading anyone else’s chart. They state the window for every rate unasked. And they notice that their decision usually turns on something more tractable than the profession’s fate: vacancy cost, ramp time, apprenticeship design.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 8 October 2026 Oindrila kept all nine requisitions but rewrote what they were. The four associate seats became a two-year programme whose first-year work is reviewing, testing and editing machine-produced artefacts rather than producing them. She would publish Rupak’s stock-flow and intensity tables every six months, with two tripwires: if intensity falls below 8.00 per hundred engineers, or screen-to-loop conversion below 12 per cent for two consecutive windows, the programme is reviewed.

Pradyumna did the opposite for the same reason. He hired one senior PM for the firmware release train at the ₹46 lakh band, paying a premium to compress the 97-day fill, because ₹18 lakh a week made every day of search expensive. He lent the second seat’s scope to Ryoko Hasegawa’s team in Osaka for two quarters, and took a campus associate for the third, where the slip meter did not run.

Three questions. First: the two protagonists reached opposite conclusions from one evidence base. Is one wrong, or is the evidence silent on what divides them, and if silent, what makes a decision defensible rather than arbitrary? Second: intensity rose 41.0 per cent at Rupak while engineering headcount fell 17.9 per cent; name the evidence that would most change your reading of that. Third: which of the four quantities would firms refuse to report?

13. Going deeper

When building gets cheap and deciding does not is the mechanism beneath every claim here. Which PM skills repriced, up and down names what a requisition now asks for; what a junior PM should learn first now is the operational form of Oindrila’s decision; which PM paths are more and less exposed breaks the profession into segments. Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn’t explains why the decision rate may not fall, and velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved supplies the test. The prototype as the new specification and what a PRD becomes when the reader can build describe the task bundle that replaced the junior seat’s. Reviewing work you did not write is the skill Rupak’s programme rests on, and taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill names what the market may be bidding for.

AI & Data Products › How AI Is Changing PM Practice

1. A cohort under review

On Monday, 6 October 2025, Farida Kulkarni, head of product at Gulmohar Marketplace Network, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. Gulmohar, a Pune-based marketplace connecting 1,40,000 artisan sellers with urban buyers, planned to hire 24 associate product managers (APMs: entry-level product managers recruited as a cohort and rotated across teams) for a January 2026 intake. The board's budget meeting was on Monday, 20 October, fourteen days away.

In one week Gagan Deshmukh, the chief people officer, had forwarded her three items: a newsletter headline announcing that product-management jobs were disappearing, a founder's post insisting that nothing had changed, and a finance request to trim the cohort to 16. Each APM carried a loaded annual cost (salary plus benefits, recruiting and equipment) of ₹18 lakh, so the request was not trivial.

Exhibit 1. The decision in rupees
OptionAPM rolesLoaded cost per APM (₹ lakh)Annual cost (₹ lakh)
Full cohort2418432
Finance proposal1618288
Difference818144

Difference = full cohort less finance proposal. All figures in ₹ lakh; 144 lakh is ₹1.44 crore.

Both errors were costly. Cut too deep, and Gulmohar would be short of mid-level product managers in 2027, when this cohort would have grown into them. Hire too many, and it would carry ₹144 lakh a year for roles the market was telling it to question. Farida asked her analyst, Eklavya Sawant, a narrower question than the headlines posed: what, exactly, has been measured?

2. The idea: a claim is only as good as its measure

The question underneath the newsletter is whether product management is a shrinking profession or merely feels like one. Answering it requires a discipline rather than a theory: separate what is measured from what is asserted, and say which rung of evidence each claim stands on. A posting is an advertisement for a role. A hire is a person who actually starts. A denominator is the base a count is compared against (all technology postings, say). Composition is the mix inside a total, such as junior versus senior. A counterfactual is what would have happened without the suspected cause.

The discipline is borrowed from labour economics, which learned long ago not to confuse openings with hires. The United States’ Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey, begun in 2000, reports openings, hires and separations as distinct series for exactly that reason. Product management has no such official series in India. Its evidence is scraped postings, professional-profile data, salary surveys and anecdote, each answering a slightly different question.

The sentence Farida could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: “A posting count tells us what employers advertised, not who was hired, and neither tells us what the profession will need.”

The ladder shows why the debate is so loud and so inconclusive: the cheapest evidence sits at the bottom, and almost nothing is reliably available at the top.

3. How it works, step by step

Eklavya’s method had six steps, several of which analysts usually leave implicit. First, define the population. Does “PM” mean anyone titled product manager, or anyone doing product work, including “product owner” and “AI product lead”? He chose titles plus a short synonym list and wrote the list down. Second, choose the measure. Third, fix a denominator, so that a fall in PM roles can be told apart from a fall in everything. Fourth, split by level. Fifth, correct for duplicates, since one vacancy reposted three times is one role. Sixth, compare to a baseline and ask what else changed between the two periods.

Exhibit 3. Five measures and what each misses
MeasureWhat it countsWhat it misses
PostingsAdvertised vacanciesReposts, ghost roles, unadvertised referral hires
HiresNew joiners in profile dataPeople who do not update profiles; lag of months
Pay by levelPrice of the workOffers that are never published
Applications per openingSupply pressureQuality of applicants
AnecdoteOne person’s experienceEveryone else

The table explains why Eklavya began with postings: they are the only series he could obtain across three job boards for two years. He did so knowing it sat on the second rung, and he labelled every chart accordingly.

4. A worked example, line by line

Eklavya compared postings in the third quarter of 2024 with the third quarter of 2025 for Indian product companies, split by level.

Exhibit 4. PM postings by level, Q3 2024 and Q3 2025
LevelQ3 2024Q3 2025ChangeChange (%)
Associate / APM1,240930−310−25.0
PM2,6102,480−130−5.0
Senior PM and above1,4501,530+80+5.5
Total5,3004,940−360−6.8

Totals are exact sums of the rows. Percentages are rounded to one decimal place.

Read line by line: postings fell 360 on a base of 5,300, or 6.8 per cent. But that average hides the story. Associate roles fell 25.0 per cent (310 of 1,240), mid-level roles 5.0 per cent, and senior roles rose 5.5 per cent. The associate share of all PM postings fell from 23.4 per cent (1,240 of 5,300) to 18.8 per cent (930 of 4,940). The effect, if real, is concentrated at the entry level.

The denominator matters too. All technology postings in the same sample were 53,000 in 2024 and 46,000 in 2025, a fall of 13.2 per cent. PM’s share of the total therefore rose from 10.0 per cent (5,300 of 53,000) to 10.7 per cent (4,940 of 46,000). Product management shrank less than the market around it.

Second pass: change one input. Raw postings include reposts. Suppose each vacancy appeared on average 1.25 times in 2024, so unique roles were 5,300 divided by 1.25, or 4,240. If reposting rose to 1.30 times in 2025, unique roles were 4,940 divided by 1.30, or 3,800. If instead it stayed at 1.25, unique roles were 3,952.

Exhibit 6. Unique PM roles under two reposting assumptions

One assumption moves the decline from 6.8 to 10.4 per cent, a swing of 3.6 percentage points. Gulmohar’s own data pointed the other way on a different dimension: applications for its 24 APM roles rose from 18,000 in 2024 to 31,200 in 2025, or from 750 to 1,300 per role, an increase of 73.3 per cent. Fewer roles and more applicants make entry-level hiring feel much worse than the postings alone suggest.

5. Nuances a learner must know

Postings are not hires

A posting is an intention; a hire is a transaction. Companies advertise roles they never fill, and fill roles they never advertise through referrals. The two series can diverge for a year.

Level matters more than the total

Exhibit 4 shows a flat-looking total hiding a quarter fall at the bottom. Any claim about “PM jobs” without a level split is almost uninterpretable.

Titles drift

If companies rename product managers as “product owners” or “AI product leads”, a title search shows a decline that is only relabelling. Whoever publishes a number should publish the title list.

Cycle and structure look alike

A hiring fall may reflect a funding slowdown, which reverses, or a change in how products are built, which does not. Postings alone cannot separate the two; only a longer series, and a comparison with unrelated roles, can begin to.

The sample is not the market

Three job boards over-represent venture-funded product companies and under-represent global capability centres (the India offices of multinationals) and IT-services firms, which hire many product managers by other routes.

Supply moves too

Applications per opening rose 73.3 per cent at Gulmohar. A rising supply of applicants makes entry harder even where demand is unchanged.

Evidence about the past is not a forecast

These tables describe twelve months. They cannot tell Farida what product teams will look like in 2028. They can only tell her whether the argument for cutting has any support yet.

Questions to ask before relying on a number

Who counted? Which titles? Compared with what? At which level? Over what period? Measuring postings, hires or pay?

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

Exhibit 7. Where the measurement problem bites
SettingTypical patternMeasurement trap
ConsumerLarge, visible product teams; heavy graduate recruitingReposting and campus pipelines inflate postings
B2BFewer PMs, closer to engineering and salesTitles vary; roles hide under “solutions”
MarketplacePMs split across supply and demand sidesTwo teams, one headline count

At Gulmohar, a marketplace, the 24 APMs would split between seller tools and buyer experience, so a hiring fall could hit one side while the other grew. In early-stage companies the evidence is mostly founder judgement; a ten-person company has no hiring series, only a decision. In large companies, the difficulty reverses: abundant data, but internal transfers and reorganisations blur what counts as a hire.

7. Common mistakes

Treating a headline as a measurement. The symptom is a slide quoting a percentage without a source, period or level. The misunderstanding is that a confident number has been counted. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask for the title list and the denominator; most claims fail within a minute.

Reading the average. The symptom is a leader saying “PM hiring is down 7 per cent, so cut everything 7 per cent”. The misunderstanding is that the total describes each level. The diagnostic is to split by level and see whether any level moves in the total’s direction.

Choosing a story and shopping for support. The symptom is that both the collapse and no-change camps cite true numbers. The misunderstanding is that evidence can be picked to fit. The diagnostic is to write down, before looking, what result would change your mind.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Farida’s decision starts with the question “what would we need to see?” rather than “which story is right?” The analyst’s title list, sample and rung of evidence are stated on page one. Results are shown by level, with the duplicate assumption exposed so a sceptical board member can change it. The recommendation is staged to the evidence, with named tripwires, a date to look again and a stated cost of being wrong in each direction. Nobody in the room claims the evidence is better than it is.

9. What Farida decided

On 20 October 2025 she asked the board for 18 roles, not 24 or 16. Twelve APMs would start in January 2026; six more would be released for an April intake only if the same tables, re-run in the first week of January on Q4 2025 postings, showed associate postings had not fallen by more than the 25.0 per cent already observed, and applicants per role had not exceeded 1,300. Her reasoning was that the evidence supported a concentrated entry-level decline but could not distinguish cycle from structure.

Exhibit 8. The staged cohort

April 20266108Released only if tripwires hold
Total18324 

At ₹18 lakh each. The plan costs 108 lakh less than the full cohort of 432 lakh and 36 lakh more than finance’s 288 lakh.

Next, read which PM skills repriced, up and down, since what is scarce is what gets hired for, and what a junior PM should learn first now, because the entry level is where this evidence points. Two questions to sit with: if the January re-run shows the associate fall has deepened, what would you now believe about cycle versus structure, and what additional evidence would you demand? And which of your own beliefs about PM hiring sits on the bottom rung of the ladder?

Maatrika Systems: Nine Open Roles

A case on product-management hiring, and on what the evidence carries

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Wednesday 21 October 2026, Nandita Barve was still at her desk in the Maatrika Systems building in Gachibowli, Hyderabad. The board's people committee met at half past nine the next morning, and Nandita, Vice President of Product, had been asked for one recommendation: how to fill the nine product-management seats still open this year, at what levels, and from where.

Nine days later, on Friday 30 October, a second clock ran out. The campus partnership Maatrika signed in March 2023 obliged it to make four product-track offers in the November placement week at ISB and two of the IIMs; withdrawing required written notice by 30 October and forfeited the ₹24 lakh fee already paid.

On her screen were six exhibits assembled over five weeks, and the uncomfortable fact that they did not agree. One said the Indian product-management market was contracting steadily, one said it was growing, one said it had collapsed. Her own numbers said something narrower: Maatrika had stopped hiring at the bottom while telling itself it had not.

2. Maatrika Systems

Maatrika, founded in Hyderabad in 2012, sells warehouse-management, dispatch and reconciliation software to retailers, pharmaceutical distributors and third-party logistics firms. In the year ended March 2026 it reported revenue of ₹1,180 crore, about 71 per cent of it from India, and employed some 3,400 people: 310 in engineering, 48 in product management as of 1 October 2026, and the rest in implementation, support and field operations.

One earlier decision shaped everything Nandita could now propose. In August 2024, after a compensation review found the company's titles unreadable to the market, Maatrika flattened its product ladder. Associate and senior product manager were abolished; everyone became a Product Manager I, II or III, with Group PM above. The intent was clarity. The effect, two years on, was that PM I became a holding pen for campus hires, transfers from support and the occasional services-firm lateral, and benchmarking became guesswork because no competitor used the same rungs. With no junior title, nobody noticed for almost a year that the junior population was draining away.

The second constraint was contractual. On 1 April 2026 Maatrika retained Manasvi Search Partners on an exclusive mandate for all PM III and above hires: ₹8 lakh a month to 31 March 2027, or ₹96 lakh, non-cancellable.

3. The industry

The market Maatrika sells into has been reshaped twice in five years. The Open Network for Digital Commerce pushed small sellers onto shared rails; UPI and NPCI's settlement infrastructure made reconciliation a software problem; the GST e-way bill made every truck movement a data event; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act added consent duties to every client record. Quick commerce — Zepto, Swiggy Instamart and their imitators — compressed delivery promises to minutes and forced Maatrika's clients to re-architect stock positions. Reliance Retail and Flipkart built much of this in-house; Delhivery and Mahindra Logistics bought parts of it.

For talent, Maatrika competes in a market it does not price. Zoho, Freshworks, Postman and Razorpay draw from the same pool, as do the Bengaluru offices of global platforms, while Infosys and TCS supply candidates who have shipped at scale but never owned a profit-and-loss line. Nistaar Logistics Group, a better-funded rival, took two of Maatrika's product managers in September.

And then there was Navshakti Labs, founded in Pune in 2024, which sells a warehouse product overlapping perhaps sixty per cent of Maatrika's core, with 61 engineers and four product managers. In July 2026 it won Mandap Retail Collective, a four-year client worth ₹11.4 crore a year — under one per cent of revenue, and far more in the retelling. Nilesh Thakurdesai had raised Navshakti in every forum since.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In March 2023 the belief behind Mihika Rautela's campus partnership was that entry-level hiring was the cheapest source of long-tenure product managers. By late 2025 the committee filled the slots dutifully rather than enthusiastically, but nobody reopened it.

The 2024 flattening, meant to make levelling legible, instead hid a composition shift. Exhibit 1 shows the PM I population peaking at 16 at the end of FY25 and standing at 7 on 1 October 2026, a fall of 56 per cent, while the organisation as a whole went from 55 to 48, a fall of 13 per cent. Had the associate title survived, somebody would have asked about the gap a year earlier.

In January 2026, when Navshakti shipped, the internal view was that a four-person product team could not hold an enterprise warehouse roadmap. Six months later it had Mandap's business. What Nandita kept writing and deleting was whether Navshakti won because its product organisation was small and fast, or because it priced 40 per cent below Maatrika and had a founder who flew to Indore every week.

From April to September 2026 the company filled five of fourteen approved seats; Exhibit 3 shows that funnel. The risk was thought to be a thin top of funnel; the opposite happened. 7,840 applications arrived for fourteen roles, 560 per role, and the screen could not tell them apart. Of those, 5,096 of the 7,840 carried cover letters Maatrika's own detector classed as machine-generated, or 65 per cent; of the work samples returned, 71 of the 196 were flagged the same way, 36 per cent. Nandita's September summary read: we are not short of candidates; we have lost the ability to read them.

On 12 August 2026 Nilesh circulated a memo arguing that cheap code generation had moved the bottleneck from specification to decision, and that Maatrika should run at twelve engineers per product manager rather than six. Thirty-seven days later, on 18 September, two of Manasi Godbole's nine product managers resigned in one week, one to Nistaar. Manasi read that coincidence differently.

5. The people

Nandita Barve, Vice President of Product, Hyderabad, owns the recommendation and believes the real shortage is judgement, not throughput. She has not said aloud that two of the seniors she most wants are people she has already failed to hire twice, or that she doubts she can land four at any price.

Mihika Rautela, Chief People Officer, Hyderabad, signed the campus agreement and is measured on offer-acceptance rate and regretted attrition. The institutions, she argues, will remember a withdrawal for a decade. She does not mention that her FY27 goal sheet carries a campus-conversion target, or that the ₹24 lakh fee sits in her budget, not Nandita's.

Nilesh Thakurdesai, Chief Technology Officer, Bengaluru, wants the ratio moved. His engineers prototype in days and he is tired of waiting for documents describing what they have already built; he is the loudest voice for four expensive seniors over nine ordinary hires. He does not say that his own budget absorbs any product headcount he gets re-designated.

Manasi Godbole, Director of Product, Pune, manages dispatch and reconciliation with a team now down to seven. She says, correctly, that nobody can hold six surfaces and that the resignations were about span of control, not AI. She has met a recruiter twice and told no one.

Minseo Han, Customer Success Director, Seoul, carries Maatrika's largest non-India account, the cold-chain operator Mekhla Cold Chain Industries, whose February 2027 renewal contract names a dedicated Asia-Pacific product manager. She wants that seat filled senior and local, which Exhibit 6 shows costs 2.18 times a Hyderabad equivalent. She has not volunteered that Mekhla's procurement team has asked what Navshakti charges.

Nadia Wójcik, Principal Designer, Warsaw, has absorbed a growing share of what used to be product work: flows, acceptance criteria, the first cut of requirements. She wants fewer and more senior product managers, because the juniors she worked with generated review load rather than decisions. She does not say that her own promotion case grows if product shrinks.

Mateo Negrete, Staff Data Scientist, Mexico City, built the detector and is the only person who has looked hard at Exhibit 5, whose ramp medians, he keeps saying, are computed on survivors and so flatter the routes with the worst retention. He is quietly pleased his detector has reached the board, and has not tested its false-positive rate on non-native English writers.

Nikhil Sardesai, independent director and chair of the people committee, Mumbai, has heard the same AI-and-headcount argument on three other boards. He wants a decision defensible if the thesis is wrong — not the same as a hedge — and will ask Nandita what evidence would change her mind.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the only table Nandita trusts completely, and it describes one company. For the market she had three sources, below, and they disagree.

A reader wanting collapse reads Source C; one wanting no change reads Source B. Mateo's note on the exhibit is three words: different denominators throughout.

Exhibit 4 costs the three courses of action; the retainer sits in every row because it is committed.

7. Voices

"We are arguing about hiring four people out of campus while a company with four product managers in total takes our accounts. I am not saying fire anyone. I am saying the next nine hires should be people who can decide, and not nine people who can write." Nilesh Thakurdesai, product and engineering review, 29 September 2026
"My two resignations earlier this month were not about agents. One of them was carrying dispatch, returns and the Mekhla integration at once because we have not backfilled a PM I since February. Call that a ratio problem if you like. The leavers call it a workload problem." Manasi Godbole, same meeting
"On Exhibit 5: the campus median of fourteen months is measured on seven people out of eighteen. Kill the campus route because it ramps slowly and you are using a number that exists only because the slow ones left." Mateo Negrete, email to Nandita Barve, 6 October 2026
"I have run thirty-one product searches this year. The senior people you want are not applying to postings; they are being moved between four companies by people like me, and the price has gone up. If the junior market collapsed, nobody told the senior market." Nirav Lokhande, Manasvi Search Partners, call notes, 9 October 2026
"I applied in May and was rejected in eleven minutes. I have six years on a payments product and a live ONDC integration behind me. I am told the market is tough. I am not sure the market saw my application." Meghana Pathare, candidate, feedback form, July 2026

8. The options as Nandita currently sees them

Option 1: fill the approved plan. Nine seats — four PM I through the campus commitment, three PM II, two PM III — at ₹434 lakh all in. It honours the agreement and rebuilds the ladder Exhibit 1 shows has drained. It also commits Maatrika to four people whose ramp it cannot measure honestly, and does nothing about a screen that cannot read 7,840 applications. Her private objection: it hires four PM I into an organisation that has not worked out what a PM I now does.

Option 2: re-level and buy senior. Six seats — two PM II and four seniors at a 25 per cent premium — at ₹544 lakh: the most expensive option, with the fewest people. It is Nilesh's proposal and Nadia's preference, and the only one that would plausibly fill Minseo's Asia-Pacific seat. It forfeits ₹24 lakh and the campus slot, bets on a thesis Maatrika has one year of evidence for, and assumes four premium seniors can be hired at all — which Nirav's index in Exhibit 2 and his remark in section 7 jointly make doubtful.

Option 3: internal apprenticeship. Nine seats — six converts from implementation, support and analytics into PM I and PM II, plus three external PM III — at ₹472 lakh including a ₹22 lakh programme. Exhibit 5 gives internal transfers the best retention of any route, 8 of 9, and a nine-month median ramp. It forfeits the campus slot, pulls six people from functions already short-staffed before the Diwali peak, and rests on nine cases, four of them Manasi's own picks.

Underneath all three she had written, in pencil: none of these is a decision about selection. Every option assumes the process that produced 11 offers and 5 acceptances will fill whatever is approved. Mateo had costed a supervised live exercise at ₹6 lakh; nobody put it in any option, because headcount was what the committee had asked about. Possibly the framing itself was the mistake.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The committee meets on 22 October. The campus notice falls due on 30 October and placement week is in November, inside the Diwali shipping peak when no client will tolerate a slipped release. The ₹96 lakh retainer is sunk and exclusive: any PM III hired outside Manasvi before 31 March 2027 triggers a fee dispute. The FY27 incremental budget for product is ₹540 lakh, which accommodates Options 1 and 3 but not Option 2 without a supplementary approval Nikhil would carry to the full board. A 2020 policy nobody has revisited requires any frozen level to stay frozen for a full financial year. And 19 of the 48 people now in product joined after August 2024, and have never seen the company hire at the bottom.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1 alone, what can Maatrika establish about product-management hiring and what remains an assertion? What would it need before it could support a claim about the market rather than one company?
  2. Exhibit 2 holds three series moving in different directions. Reconstruct what each counts and decide which, if any, bears on the decision. Is the disagreement a data problem or a definition problem?
  3. Exhibit 3 reports 7,840 applications and five acceptances. Which stage binds, and does the machine-generated-cover-letter finding change your answer or merely decorate it?
  4. Exhibit 5 is the strongest evidence for Option 3 and, as Mateo argues, possibly the weakest exhibit in the pack. How would you repair it, and what if the repair reversed the ranking of the routes?
  5. Nilesh's twelve-to-one ratio and Navshakti's fifteen-to-one both appear in Figure 1. What would have to be true of Maatrika's products, clients and regulatory surface for either to be right? For neither?
  6. What should Nandita recommend on 22 October, what should she say when Nikhil Sardesai asks what evidence would change her mind, and what should she do about the campus notice eight days later if the committee declines to decide?

Later that night

Nandita closed the deck at ten to one and did not send it. What she could not get past was that every version of her recommendation was a claim about the future of her profession, built from three years of one company's records, two conflicting market indices and a third she had been told to discount, and a ramp table whose headline number described eleven people no longer there. She believed, on balance, that the entry level had repriced; she also believed she could not prove it, that Nilesh's certainty was worth less than it sounded, and that Mihika's loyalty to the institutions was not merely sentimental. The November slot would go to somebody. Whether to four of her own product managers, or to nobody, she had not decided.

Which PM paths are more and less exposed

AI & Data Products, How AI Is Changing PM Practice

1. Six names and a spreadsheet

On Thursday 12 March 2026, Chitra Anantharaman, head of product at Aranya Systems in Pune, opened a spreadsheet with six names in it. Six associate product managers had accepted offers to join on 1 July 2026. Each would cost ₹18 lakh a year fully loaded, ₹108 lakh in total. The chief executive, Cyrus Batliwala, wanted all six placed on Aranya Desk, the workflow product with the longest backlog. Chitra's existing fourteen PMs were spread unevenly across three lines.

Exhibit 1. Aranya's PM team before the intake, March 2026.

Abhijeet Nadkarni, the head of engineering, had run a two-week trial. An AI assistant produced first-draft specifications for Desk in under an hour that a junior PM needed a day to write. Nobody could say which line would still need six juniors in three years, and the placements had to be confirmed by 20 April, 39 days away.

If she chose badly, six people would spend their formative years on the work being repriced fastest, and the better ones would leave. Chitra decided early that she would not try to forecast which tools would win. She would ask a narrower question: in which line does the work that remains, after the tools have taken their share, concentrate the most judgement, domain knowledge and accountability?

2. The idea

This page uses two terms. The exposure of a PM path is the share of its working hours spent on tasks that current AI tools can do to an acceptable standard with light human review. A hedge is a choice made so that you are not ruined if a forecast is wrong. The career hedge here is a path whose remaining hours concentrate three things: judgement (choosing between options when the evidence conflicts), domain knowledge (facts about a regulated industry, a physical product or a platform's ecosystem that sit in few public documents), and accountability (a named person who answers when the decision goes wrong).

The problem it solves is that forecasts about whole occupations are usually wrong in a useful direction. Jobs are bundles of tasks, an argument made in 2003 by the economists David Autor, Frank Levy and Richard Murnane. Carl Frey and Michael Osborne estimated occupation-level automation probabilities in 2013, and in 2023 Tyna Eloundou and colleagues applied a task-level exposure measure to language models. A PM job is a bundle too, and the bundle has parts that reprice at very different speeds.

Figure 1 shows the whole method. Hours are weighted by how replaceable each task is, and the residue is examined for who holds it. The sentence Chitra could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "We are not betting on which tool wins; we are choosing where an error is expensive and someone has to sign their name to it."

3. How it actually works

The method has four steps, and the second and fourth are the ones practitioners usually leave implicit.

Step one: record the week. Job descriptions flatter. Chitra and Abhijeet had three PMs per line, nine in all, keep a time diary for two weeks, sorting each hour into six task categories. The categories were drafting specifications, synthesising feedback and data, status updates, prioritisation under conflicting constraints, negotiating with regulators, auditors or suppliers, and owning outcomes after launch.

Step two: score each task by testing it. The implicit part is the phrase "acceptable standard". Here it meant: would the person who signs this work release it after a ten-minute review? The team ran the assistant on real Aranya artefacts and scored what survived review, rather than guessing from demonstrations.

Step three: multiply and sum. Each task's hours are multiplied by its substitutability, and the products are added. This gives exposed hours, which are divided by total hours to give exposure.

Step four: inspect the residue. The unexposed hours are not simply safe. The question is who is accountable for them and whether that accountability transfers to a tool. A calculation that stops at step three measures workload; step four turns it into a career decision.

4. A worked example

Exhibit 2 gives the averaged time-diary hours for a 40-hour week on each line, with the substitutability scores from the trial. Taking Desk as the line to follow: drafting contributes 10 × 0.70 = 7.00 exposed hours, synthesis 8 × 0.80 = 6.40, status 6 × 0.75 = 4.50, prioritisation 8 × 0.30 = 2.40, regulator or supplier work 3 × 0.10 = 0.30, and post-launch ownership 5 × 0.15 = 0.75. The sum is 21.35 hours, or 53.4 per cent of 40.

Lend gains 8 × 0.20 = 1.60, reaching 18.55 (46.4 per cent). Reader gains 6 × 0.20 = 1.20, reaching 15.90 (39.8 per cent).

Every line gets worse, and the ranking does not change. The gap between Desk and Reader widens from 16.6 to 18.6 points (53.375 less 36.75, then 58.375 less 39.75). The result Chitra took from this is that the ordering is robust to a changed input, while the levels are not. She trusted the ordering and distrusted the levels.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Exposure is not displacement

A line with 53.4 per cent exposure does not lose 53.4 per cent of its PMs. Cheaper drafting may raise demand for products, or move the saved hours to other tasks. Exposure describes where the price of work is falling, not who is dismissed.

Hours are not value

One decision on a lending policy can matter more than forty hours of status reports. An hours-weighted index understates how much of a path's worth sits in its few unexposed hours, and that is why step four exists.

Scores decay and are local

A substitutability score is a measurement of one tool on one team's artefacts in one month. Re-run it each quarter. A score from another company's blog is a rumour.

Accountability is not domain knowledge

A PM who knows lending rules but does not sign off on them holds knowledge that a tool can partly replicate. A PM who answers to the compliance head for a product's behaviour holds accountability that cannot be handed over. They overlap, but only the second is hard to automate by design.

Regulated does not mean safe

A path is hedged only if the PM actually does the regulator-facing and audit-facing work. A PM in a lending company who spends every hour drafting tickets has the exposure of a Desk PM with a better title.

Seniority changes the mix

Juniors spend a larger share of their hours on the replaceable tasks, so their exposure sits above the line average. The hedge has to include a route to the residue: how and when the junior starts to carry accountability.

"AI product PM" is not automatically a hedge

Building AI features is a popular specialisation, which means competition for it is crowded. It is hedged only where the domain, the failure cost or the regulator makes the judgement scarce.

ConsumerTrust and safety, pricing fairness, and taste; high volume of cheap experiments, so more hours are exposed

Consumer products tend to be more exposed because their work is experiment-heavy, artefact-heavy and quick to iterate. B2B work holds judgement in contracts and in customer relationships, where a named person is expected to pick up the telephone. Marketplace work holds it in policy, which decides who gains and who loses between two groups of users.

Company size changes the mix further. In an early-stage company of twenty people one PM does everything, so exposure is the blended average, but that person is also accountable for everything. In a large company the replaceable tasks are the ones most likely to be pooled into a central team or tool, which can leave a junior PM with a thin residue.

7. Common mistakes

Choosing by headline. The symptom is a team moving everyone to the path with the most press coverage. The misunderstanding is that visibility equals scarcity. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask who would sign the decision in that path, and whether you can name them.

Treating the index as a forecast. The symptom is a slide that says "Desk: 53.4 per cent, avoid". The misunderstanding is that a snapshot of task prices describes the future. The diagnostic is to re-run the second pass with a deliberately worse input, and see whether the decision changes.

Confusing a sector with a skill. The symptom is a PM who takes a lending job and still spends 30 of 40 hours drafting. The misunderstanding is that the sector confers the hedge. The diagnostic is a two-week time diary, taken before and after the move.

Ignoring the junior route. The symptom is a cohort that does only exposed work for two years. The misunderstanding is that the residue will arrive with tenure. The diagnostic is to ask what accountable task each junior carries by month six.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version has a short sequence. The team keeps time diaries before it argues. It tests substitutability on its own artefacts, and tells everyone which scores are measured and which are guessed. It states the ordering and the levels separately, and it sets a date to repeat the test. Crucially, it places each junior with a named senior who carries the accountable work, and it gives the junior a small, real piece of that work within six months. The decision is written down in a page that someone outside the team could audit.

9. What Chitra decided

Chitra rejected Cyrus's proposal of six on Desk. She placed two PMs on each line. Desk would grow from 7 to 9, Lend from 4 to 6, and Reader from 3 to 5, a total of 20. Each of the two on Desk would spend a quarter of their time on Lend's compliance reviews, so that their hours were not entirely drafting. She told Cyrus that she was not predicting that Desk would shrink. She was refusing to put all of ₹108 lakh a year behind one set of tasks whose price was falling, and she scheduled a re-test of the scores for the end of the next quarter.

To go further, read about choosing a PM specialisation, where the hedge becomes a concrete career choice, and about what the hiring evidence does and does not show. A hedge built on the second keeps you from building one on the discourse.

Two questions to sit with. First, in your own current week, which hours would you be least willing to hand to a tool, and is anyone else able to name why? Second, if the drafting score rose to 100 per cent, which of your tasks would you most want to be left holding?

2. The idea, and the five camps that disagree about it

A job is a bundle of tasks; automation acts on tasks, and a job's fate is the weighted sum of its tasks' fates. That decomposition is due to David Autor, Frank Levy and Richard Murnane in 2003. Carl Frey and Michael Osborne went the other way in 2013, scoring whole occupations; Melanie Arntz and colleagues re-ran it at task level in 2016 and cut the headline figure by two-thirds. Tyna Eloundou and colleagues measured task-level exposure to language models in 2023; Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo supply the mechanism by which a falling task price becomes, or fails to become, a falling wage.

Three quantities are used here. Exposure is the share of a week's hours in clusters whose unit price is falling. The repricing rate, ρ, is the hours-weighted annual change in the market price of an hour of a role's work: a price, not a probability of dismissal. Accountable share, α, is the fraction of the week spent on work terminating in a decision a named person signs. A career hedge is a position taken so that being wrong about which tools win does not ruin you; like any hedge it carries a premium, usually paid in forgone upside. Alan Blinder's 2006 work on offshorability is the nearest precedent: the useful split was not skill but whether a service had to be delivered in person, and accountability plays that role here.

Measure the person, not the path

ρ is a price, not a probability of dismissal

A hedge has a premium, usually paid in upside

The tell is “we are in insurance, so we are fine.” Nivaaran's Provider Portal, at −17.0 per cent, sits inside one of the most supervised industries in India. Regulation buys slower diffusion, postponing repricing rather than preventing it — decisive over twenty years, negligible over three.

The tell is a cluster priced over eight months beside one priced over two years in the same column. Annualising a short window during fast tool change produces rates that are artefacts of the start date, and the error then compounds.

Platform work is intermediate: a published interface is irreversible, and deprecation is among the least automatable things a PM does. 8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

A cohort with no accountable work. Early sign: associates who cannot name a decision of theirs that could have gone wrong. Diagnostic: by month six, what does each junior sign? Nivaaran's cost was ₹55 lakh in replacements and an empty promotion bench.

Letting the centre absorb the residue. Early sign: a shared-services group with “excellence” in its name. Diagnostic: after the change, who signs? Manthan's version would have cost 4.7 points of ρ across every instrument PM.

Treating the index as permanent. Early sign: a rate column older than two quarters with no re-measurement date. Diagnostic: when is the panel re-priced?

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Does the residue appreciate, or merely resist? The appreciation case is Baumol-style: as exposed work gets cheap, the scarce complement commands more, which is what the +4 per cent on accountable ownership shows. It fails if accountability becomes tradeable — if model-risk insurance, regulator-accepted attestation, or indemnity-bearing vendors let a company buy the signature rather than employ it. There are early signs of all three.

Is the hedge a trap? The strongest version is not that the hedged path pays less but that the exposed work is the apprenticeship: the judgement in cluster four is built by having drafted two hundred specifications badly. If so, a junior who hedges early arrives at thirty-five with high α and thin judgement. The evidence is the novice-gain literature and the fact that senior PMs' instincts were trained on work that no longer exists. It would be wrong if judgement can be acquired from reviewing machine output at volume — plausible, unproven, the most consequential open question here.

Mix or diffusion? The mix camp points at Portal 57.080 against Insight 56.982 and declares sector irrelevant. The diffusion camp answers that panels price the present, and that supervised industries adopt late for structural reasons — validation, audit trails, liability — so the same mix in a regulated business reprices years behind its unregulated twin. Both are right about different horizons; the question is whether your hedge must survive three years or twenty.

Hours or decisions? The taste camp holds the unit is wrong: what is scarce is selecting one option from forty cheap ones, an act occupying minutes and determining everything. They would replace the diary with an inventory of consequential decisions per quarter. Nobody has published a workable version — a point against the proposal, not an argument for the diary.

11. What mastery looks like

Three behaviours separate the internalised version from the studied one. Such a person talks about weeks rather than jobs, and asks for a calendar before discussing a path. They separate ordering from levels out loud, and set a re-measurement date before presenting a first result. And they treat the distribution of accountable hours as chosen on behalf of other people's careers, not a by-product of the backlog. The studied version produces an index; the internalised version produces a diary, a price panel, a signature list and a date.

12. What each protagonist decided

Lalitha Muthuraman took a plan to the board on 13 March 2026 that gave Lohiya less than he wanted and Narkhede less than she wanted. Four of the nine went to the Adjudication Core, two to the Provider Portal and three to Shield, taking the organisation from 13 PMs to 22: Core from 5 to 9, Portal from 6 to 8, Shield from 2 to 5. Lohiya's proposal put seven of the nine on the Portal and one each elsewhere: Core 6, Portal 13 and Shield 3 — the same 22 heads, distributed the other way. The grade mix and the ₹2.52 crore were unchanged; she was refusing to put three-quarters of it behind a 16.7 per cent α. The two associates went to the Core on a condition written into the plan: each would own one named rule family, countersigned by Narkhede, within six months. She told the board she was not forecasting that the Portal would shrink, and expected its headcount to grow.

Nachiket Modak answered Mungekar on 26 February 2026, a day before his deadline, accepting Manthan Insight on condition that the CPCB compliance reporting move to him and that the certification hours stay with the instrument PMs rather than a central group. Mungekar agreed to the first and deferred the second to the June planning cycle, which Modak recorded in writing. Marieke Nijhuis in Rotterdam, who handled the European distributor, and Nurul Mazlan in Kuala Lumpur, who ran regional service, were told the reasoning in those terms, because the arrangement only works if the people around a signatory know who signs.

Three questions for discussion. First, Shield had no diary: was excluding it from the measurement and then funding it most aggressively a defensible inconsistency, or a preferred answer by another route? Second, if the apprenticeship objection holds, were the two associates helped or harmed by the least exposed line in the company? Third, Modak took accountability for an obligation he had never performed: what is the strongest case that he bought a hedge, and the strongest that he bought a liability?

13. Going deeper

Which PM skills repriced, up and down supplies the rate column this page consumes; without it ρ is a guess dressed as arithmetic. Choosing a PM specialisation is where the hedge becomes a job title accepted or declined, and PM hiring: what the evidence says and what it doesn't keeps that choice built on data rather than discourse. When building gets cheap and deciding does not explains the sign on cluster six; Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't explains why cluster two repriced at −20 per cent while the evidence behind it did not. The prototype as the new specification and What a PRD becomes when the reader can build account for the −24 per cent on drafting. Reviewing work you did not write is the craft the apprenticeship objection turns on, and Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved corrects teams that mistake cheaper hours for faster outcomes.

A case on where judgement, domain knowledge and accountability concentrate.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, 11 October 2026, Kalyani Shirgaonkar sat at the dining table of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with a spreadsheet of twenty-one rows, one per product manager at Lipi Software Works, and a column she had hidden. It was headed exposed.

The mandate of 6 October set a payroll run-rate of ₹5.40 crore against the ₹7.21 crore the bench costs today — a cut of ₹181 lakh, or 25.1 per cent. Her draft, Exhibit 2, came in at ₹5.73 crore. She had spent the evening looking for ₹33 lakh and found a question instead: not who was good, but which of them stood on ground that would still be there in three years, and whether she herself stood on any. 2. The company, and one decision that will not let go

Lipi was founded in Pune in 2013 by two former Infosys engineers who had noticed that every large Indian enterprise ran on documents nobody could find. It is now 2,400 people, with revenue of ₹1,180 crore in the year to March 2026, up from ₹1,041 crore, a rise of 13.4 per cent. The workflow suite, ₹742 crore of the ₹1,180 crore total, or 62.9 per cent, grew 6.0 per cent; lending and compliance software for non-banking financial companies reached ₹196 crore and grew 34.2 per cent; platform and integrations reached ₹142 crore and grew 40.6 per cent; a device line reached ₹58 crore.

Two earlier decisions bind her tonight. In March 2023 Lipi won a five-year agreement with Kusum Retail Collective worth ₹118 crore, or ₹23.6 crore a year, two per cent of revenue, running to March 2028. To win it, Lipi conceded a clause nobody thought mattered: two named product owners from a client-approved list, with ninety days' notice and written consent before either is replaced. Both are senior product managers on the workflow suite — on paper her most movable people, in fact her least.

In July 2024 the company centralised the craft: requirement documents, research synthesis, release notes, teardowns and the weekly status pack moved into a Product Operations pod of six, so that line managers would be freed for strategy. In January 2026 Lipi rolled out an assistant that drafted all five artefacts tolerably well, and the pod found itself holding exactly the work that had just repriced. Four of the six remain; Kirtida Dalal is one.

3. The industry around the decision

Indian enterprise software in 2026 was not short of demand; it was short of patience. Zoho and Freshworks had set a price expectation that made every feature conversation a cost conversation, and Infosys, TCS and Wipro were bundling workflow automation into deals at margins Lipi could not match. Where the growth sat was where the rules sat. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions required a named accountable owner for every automated credit decision and the preservation of its reasoning; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's consent-manager rules had turned data-flow design into a documented obligation; the account aggregator framework, GST e-invoicing, ONDC's network policies and SEBI's conduct rules each produced software that could not ship without somebody putting a name on it. Lipi's lending customers, Kuber Capital Services among them, did not buy features; they bought the ability to answer an inspector. The device line carried accountability of another kind: Lohit Devices Industries put Lipi firmware on meters for state distribution companies and controllers for electric fleets, where Ather and Ola Electric had made the Bureau of Indian Standards a product constraint.

Lipi's exposure was global too: Lukasz Baran ran customer success from Warsaw, Lam Thanh Group in Ho Chi Minh City was the first large Asian account outside India, and Linnea Holmberg's designers in Stockholm and Kyungmi Rhee's data scientists in Seoul sat on bands two to three times the Bengaluru equivalent.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

At each point in the sequence of Figure A the company believed something it no longer believes. In January 2026 the assistant went live, and the belief was that product managers would be freed for judgement. In April finance restructured the time-tracking task codes so a feature would carry its full cost: drafting inside a feature ticket would now book to the feature, not the drafting code. Nobody connected this to headcount.

On 3 August the board asked for a plan on product-management cost, and Kedar said he would bring evidence rather than opinion. Kalyani ran a four-week time diary from 1 to 28 September in which product managers logged their hours against five categories; eighteen of the twenty-one completed all four weeks. That is Exhibit 1. On 1 October, with the quarter closed, Kedar circulated a dashboard comparing hours booked by task code in July to September 2025 against 2026. That is Exhibit 6.

They do not agree. The diary says 1,924 of the 3,768 hours logged, 51.1 per cent, still sat in the bundles that have repriced downward: drafting, synthesis, status and coordination. The dashboard says only 2,808 of the 7,800 booked hours in the 2026 quarter, 36.0 per cent, sat in those codes, and that drafting fell 62.0 per cent year on year.

What turned out to be wrong is simpler than either story. Booking compliance — hours booked as a share of chargeable hours available — was 90.9 per cent in the 2025 quarter and 68.0 per cent in 2026, and the April restructuring removed the code people had used for most of their drafting. If all 3,666 hours left unbooked in 2026 were drafting, the exposed share would be 56.5 per cent, above the diary's figure; if none were, the dashboard is right. Nobody knows, because the data that would settle it was redefined mid-window.

5. The people

Kalyani Shirgaonkar, 37, senior director of product, Bengaluru, built the lending line from two people to four before handing it over. Position: the four new roles must be the accountable ones, even at the cost of two workflow seats. Incentive, split: Kedar has offered her the workflow vice-presidency, eleven of the fifteen seats, or a directorship of a four-person regulated and platform group at a quarter of the raise. Unsaid: she took the lending line in 2021 because nobody wanted it, and cannot tell whether she believes it safer or wants to be right.

Kedar Bhagwat, 52, chief product officer, Bengaluru, commissioned the dashboard and presents it. Position: the bench should shrink and the saving should fund engineering. Incentive: a long-term plan measuring product and engineering cost against revenue. Unsaid: it vests in fourteen months, and he has not read the booking-compliance footnote on his own exhibit.

Latika Mascarenhas, 41, vice-president of engineering, Pune, says her senior engineers now write better requirement documents than most PMs and would rather have two staff engineers than four PMs. Unsaid: two of her best left for Krama Network in August and she needs a visible win.

Kirtida Dalal, 29, of the Product Operations pod, is the strongest writer on the bench and, by the diary, the most exposed person in the company. She wants the lending-owner role and will leave if kept in the pod. Unsaid: she holds an offer from Kavach Compliance Labs at lower pay, and has never been accountable to a regulator.

Lavin Dastur, 34, senior product manager, lending and compliance, Mumbai, already does what the new role would formalise and argues that naming an owner makes one person carry what a committee should. Unsaid: in June he signed an attestation on a credit decision he did not fully understand.

Kumud Parab, 45, human resources business partner, Hyderabad, holds that ten exits in a quarter will be noticed and that policy requires affected employees be offered internal roles first. Unsaid: she has been told to model a second reduction for April 2027.

Linnea Holmberg, 38, design director, Stockholm, has watched three design roles become one and argues the survivor is the role that owns the decision, not the artefact. Unsaid: her own 2027 headcount request was refused. Option A — protect the revenue centre. Keep the workflow bench whole and open only two of the four new roles, dropping model evaluation and device. The slate falls to ₹480.0 lakh across thirteen seats, ₹60.0 lakh under the mandate, and implies the workflow vice-presidency. The cost: the two highest-exposure groups in Exhibit 1 stay the bulk of her organisation.

Option B — build the hedge. Open all four new roles, funded by cutting one more PM and one more senior PM from the workflow suite. The slate falls to ₹500.0 lakh across thirteen seats, ₹40.0 lakh under the mandate. This is the shape Exhibit 5 and Figure B appear to argue for, and it implies the four-person directorship. The cost: cutting into the line that pays for everything, in a year it grew 6.0 per cent.

Option C — hold the draft and ask for the money. Submit fifteen seats at ₹573.0 lakh, declare the ₹33.0 lakh overshoot, and argue that the mandate was set against a dashboard whose denominator changed in April — putting her on the wrong side of the only evidence Kedar has shown the board.

Beneath the three she had added a fourth line she could not turn into an option. What if the paths are not the unit?
