If that is right, all three options answer a question about where to stand when the question is what the seat is made of.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Six constraints bind the slate, due at nine on Monday, 12 October 2026 and going to the board on 22 October.

Money. ₹540.0 lakh of run-rate against a draft of ₹573.0 lakh, plus the one-time severance of Exhibit 3, at least ₹80.0 lakh and up to ₹160.0 lakh. Contract. The Kusum agreement names two product owners, both senior PMs on the workflow suite; replacing either needs ninety days' notice and written client consent, which, counted from Monday, cannot complete before 10 January 2027 — after the slate takes effect. Two of the four retained senior seats are pre-assigned.

Regulation. Lending customers now ask for the accountable owner's name in writing during due diligence; the role can be blank on a chart, not in practice. Policy. The four new roles must be offered internally first. Kirtida is internal. So is Lavin, who does not want it.

People. Ten exits, including three associate PMs with fourteen to twenty-six months of experience; Exhibit 4 shows the fast-closing paths paying a median of ₹28 to ₹31 lakh. Evidence. The only quantitative document the board has seen is Exhibit 6, and contradicting it means explaining the April task-code change to a board with fourteen other items on its agenda.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Rank the six lines in Exhibit 1 by exposure. What does the exposed-share column measure, and how could it be wrong in each direction?
  2. Exhibits 6 and 1 give exposed shares of 36.0 per cent and 51.1 per cent for overlapping populations. Which, if either, would you put before the board?
  3. Exhibits 4 and 5 disagree about the market's shape. What does each answer well, and what would you collect instead?
  4. Kedar's, Latika's and Kirtida's incentives align on at least one element of the slate. Where, and is that alignment evidence or noise?
  5. If the unit of exposure is the seat's accountability rather than the market it sells into, how would you redraw Exhibit 1 — and would it change the slate, her own choice, or both?
  6. What does she submit at nine on Monday: which fifteen seats, which four roles, and how is the ₹33.0 lakh resolved? Then write the three sentences she would say to the board, one of them about Exhibit 6, and name what she is betting her own career on.

At twenty past midnight Kalyani unhid the column again. The pod was 75.0 and the device line was 25.0, and those people sat on the same floor. She thought about Lavin's phrase — a liability with a title — and about Linnea's line that the surviving role is the one where the deciding cannot be moved, and could not tell whether the two disagreed.

She opened a blank document, typed Recommended slate — 12 October, and underneath it the only line she was sure of: the evidence we have was built for other questions. In eight hours and forty minutes she would have to send something.

Three Offers and a Hedge: Chetana Sarin’s Next Three Years

A teaching case on which product management paths are more and less exposed to AI-driven change

1. Opening

On Sunday, 11 October 2026, Chetana Sarin sat on the floor of her rented room in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with three offer letters printed out and a fourth sheet of paper that she had written herself. The fourth sheet had a single question at the top: where will the judgement be in 2029? She had graduated from the Indian School of Business in the spring, after four years as a software engineer at Infosys. Three offers had arrived within eight days, they pointed in three directions, and every conversation about them turned into an argument about artificial intelligence.

All three offers expired on Friday, 16 October. She would have to accept one and decline two. What troubled her was not the money, which was close, but a sentence her professor had used in a class on how AI is changing PM practice: “Do not bet your career on predicting which tool wins. Bet on where accountability sits.”

2. Company background

Bharosa Credit Services is a Mumbai-based non-banking financial company that lends to small merchants, with a loan book of about ₹6,000 crore and a product team of 14. Like Bajaj Finance and Tata Capital, it works within RBI’s digital lending directions and the DPDP Act. It offered Chetana a product manager role on merchant underwriting.

Chamak Labs is a Bengaluru start-up, 90 people, that sells an AI writing and meeting-notes assistant to small businesses. It competes with offerings from Zoho and Freshworks as well as global tools, and its product is built on model interfaces rented from outside vendors. It offered her a role as product manager for the assistant’s core features.

Bijli Devices Industries is a Pune manufacturer of smart electricity meters and charging controllers, selling to state distribution companies and to makers of electric two-wheelers such as Ather and Ola Electric. Its 400 staff include a firmware team and a BIS certification group. It offered her a role managing a charger-controller line.

3. The situation

Chetana distrusted the discourse, which offered confident claims both that product managers would be replaced and that nothing would change. Rather than pick a camp, she wrote down what she could observe: how each role’s week would actually be spent, and, across 120 PM job listings posted in September, where employers named domain or regulatory knowledge. Exhibit 1 sets out the offers. Exhibit 2 is her estimate of the working week in each role, built from interviews with the three hiring managers. Exhibit 3 is the posting sample.

The three hiring managers had also told her something about repricing. At Chamak, drafting requirement documents, synthesising user feedback and preparing status updates were already done mostly by the assistant itself; the manager said these tasks no longer justified a headcount. At Bharosa, the same tools were in use, but nothing could be released until compliance and the credit risk committee signed it off, and a named person answered to RBI inspectors. At Bijli, a mistake in a charger controller meant a recall, so the PM’s role was largely to arbitrate between firmware, certification and cost.

4. The people

Bharat Venkataraman, 58, in Pune, had run product at a payments company for a decade before retiring into advisory work. He favoured the regulated role, and his reasoning was historical rather than predictive: in every technology shift he had lived through, the people who held licences, signatures and liability stayed employed longest.

Chitra Naidu, head of product at Chamak Labs in Bengaluru, was the hiring manager for offer B and an honest salesperson. She told Chetana that the learning curve at Chamak would be the steepest of the three, that she would ship weekly, and that her portfolio of shipped features would be visible to every future employer. She also admitted that a vendor release could erase part of the roadmap overnight.

Bela Hartog, in Amsterdam, was a former design lead who had retrained as a PM at an AI infrastructure company. She urged Chetana to look at platform and AI roles instead of any of the three, arguing that evaluation work, deciding what “good” means for a model, was where judgement was concentrating.

Chebet Kiprop, an ISB classmate working at a mobile-money firm in Nairobi, said little about AI and a great deal about licences. Slow regulators, she said, create stable jobs. She also warned that regulated roles could feel like compliance management, and that a bored PM leaves.

6. The options

Option A: Bharosa. The highest cash, a large share of the week in accountable work and a path that is open: 34 of the 40 regulated listings named a domain requirement. The cost is pace, and Chebet’s boredom warning was fair.

Option B: Chamak. The fastest learning, weekly shipping and a possible equity upside that no one could price. The cost is exposure: 64.4 per cent of the week sat in tasks already losing value, the lowest cash, and a vendor-dependent roadmap.

Option C: Bijli. The lowest exposed share, at 31.1 per cent, and the deepest physical and safety accountability. The cost is liquidity. Hardware is a small corner of the market, and her next move might require relocating.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, which task bundles have repriced down, and what share of each role do they occupy? Why is that a better basis for exposure than a ranking of tools?
  2. Exhibit 3 shows high domain demand in both regulated and hardware paths. Why might market size matter as much when hedging?
  3. Chitra and Bela each offer a credible reason to prefer an AI-adjacent role. What would have to be true for exposure to matter less than learning speed?
  4. If you were Chetana, which offer would you accept by 16 October, and what would you do in the first twelve months to keep your options open?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. The lens is not “which jobs will AI take?” but “where do judgement, domain knowledge and accountability concentrate?” A career hedge built on a forecast about tools fails when the forecast does. A hedge built on where a named person must answer for a decision survives changes in the tools, because the decision still needs an owner.

One defensible path. Accept Bharosa. It pays the most in cash (₹32 lakh against ₹29 lakh and ₹27 lakh), carries an accountability share of 37.8 per cent, an exposed share of 35.6 per cent, and sits in the path where 85.0 per cent of listings ask for domain knowledge and a third of the sample lives. Bijli scores slightly better on exposure at 31.1 per cent but comes from a path with only 8.3 per cent of the market, so it hedges the skill and leaves the exit narrow. Chamak trades the hedge for speed, and at 64.4 per cent exposed that is a choice she can make later, once she has a regulated base.

What makes it a hedge rather than a retreat. In her first year Chetana should volunteer for the underwriting model’s evaluation work, define what a good decision looks like, and build her own artefacts, so that she joins the regulated path while also learning the craft Bela described. She should review the choice in eighteen months against the same three exhibits, and rewrite the hours estimate with real data. Bijli is defensible for someone willing to relocate, if the reasoning rests on exposure and exit options.
